cocktails.name: Americano
cocktails.garnish: Half an orange slice and a lemon zest
instructions: Fill an old fashioned glass with ice cubes.
Pour in the Campari and sweet vermouth.
Add a splash of soda water and stir gently.
Garnish with half an orange slice and a lemon zest.
cocktails.history:
The name is Italian for "American-style". Difford's Guide links it to an American fashion for vermouth mixed with bitters, which led Italian producers to sell pre-bittered "vermouth Americano" and bars to improvise their own bittersweet blends, some lengthened with soda. As the Milano-Torino (Campari with vermouth) caught on, Campari became the preferred bitter element.

Wikipedia places the first serves at Gaspare Campari's café in Milan in the 1860s, though that date is not documented in print. The earliest recipes Difford's cites appear in Ferruccio Mazzon's 1920 Il Barista, and Elveio Grassi's 1936 Mille Misture lists around a dozen versions.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A low-strength, bittersweet aperitivo. Campari brings bitter orange peel and gentian, and the red vermouth softens it with herbal sweetness and a hint of spice. Soda lightens the body and adds a gentle fizz, so the drink is long and refreshing rather than heavy. The orange and lemon garnish adds a fresh citrus aroma that suits it to warm afternoons before a meal.

cocktails.name: Aviation
instructions: Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker.
Shake with cracked ice.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry if you like.
cocktails.history:
The Aviation first appears in print in Hugo R. Ensslin's 1916 book Recipes for Mixed Drinks. Ensslin was head bartender at the Hotel Wallick in New York and is widely credited with creating it. His version was two parts gin to one part lemon juice, sharpened with small dashes of maraschino and crème de violette.

Difford's Guide ties the name to the pale sky-blue tint the violette gives the drink and to the early days of flying, when air travel was a glamorous luxury. A 1930 version by Harry Craddock left out the violette, and Difford's lists it as a separate recipe.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A crisp gin sour with a floral edge. Fresh lemon gives a bright, tart backbone, and maraschino adds a dry, nutty cherry sweetness rather than sugariness. A small amount of crème de violette brings a soft perfumed note and a pale lilac-blue colour. The botanicals of the gin come through clearly, and the finish is clean and lightly sour.

cocktails.name: Bee's Knees
instructions: Stir the honey syrup with the lemon and orange juices until dissolved.
Add the gin and shake with ice.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
Optionally garnish with a lemon or orange zest.
cocktails.history:
For decades the Bee's Knees was described as a Prohibition-era American drink whose honey and lemon hid bad gin, an idea Difford's Guide traces to David Embury. Newer research points to Paris instead. Its first appearance in a cocktail book is the 1929 French title Cocktails de Paris, which credits Frank Meier, head bartender at the Hôtel Ritz.

A Brooklyn newspaper article from April 1929 instead credited the socialite Margaret "Molly" Brown. Difford's suggests Meier may have made it for her or at her suggestion. Meier claimed the recipe again in his 1936 book. Embury's 1948 book suggested adding a little orange juice.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bright and gently floral. Honey gives the drink a rounder, more aromatic sweetness than sugar would, and fresh lemon balances it with clean acidity. The orange juice in this spec softens the sourness and adds a juicy, slightly fruity body. Dry gin keeps a juniper backbone underneath, so the finish is fresh and only lightly sweet.

cocktails.name: Bellini
instructions: Pour the white peach purée into a mixing glass with ice.
Add the Prosecco.
Stir gently and pour into a chilled flute.
cocktails.history:
Giuseppe Cipriani created the Bellini at Harry's Bar in Venice in 1945, according to Difford's Guide, drawing on the Italian habit of steeping fresh peaches in wine. He named it after the 15th-century Venetian painter Giovanni Bellini, because the drink's pink colour reminded him of the painter's rosy tones.

In his own later account, Cipriani said he mixed fresh peach juice with Prosecco one summer, found that guests loved it, and named it during an exhibition of the painter's work. Because white peaches are seasonal, Venetian bars that refuse to use frozen purée serve it only from late spring to autumn.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Soft, fruity and lightly sparkling. Ripe white peach gives a fragrant, velvety sweetness and a pale blush colour, while Prosecco adds crisp bubbles, green-apple freshness and gentle acidity. The texture is fuller than plain sparkling wine thanks to the purée, but the drink stays low in alcohol and easy-going, a natural fit for brunch or an early aperitivo.

cocktails.name: Between the Sheets
instructions: Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker.
Shake with ice.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
The origins of this risqué-sounding drink are murky. Difford's Guide thinks it probably began in Prohibition-era America as a gin and rum drink, then took on brandy in Europe to become more like a Sidecar. Other claims point to a bartender at London's Berkeley Hotel in 1921, a New Rochelle speakeasy bartender, and Harry MacElhone in Paris.

The first printed recipe, in Frank Shay's 1929 Drawn From The Wood, used gin, rum and Cointreau. Several versions with different base spirits existed for years. The brandy, rum and triple sec version used today owes much to Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A strong, spirit-forward sour in the Sidecar family. Cognac brings warm notes of dried fruit and oak, and white rum lightens the body with a clean cane sweetness. Triple sec adds plenty of orange, and a modest measure of lemon keeps it bright without making it sharp. The result is rich, citrusy and noticeably boozy, with a smooth, slightly sweet finish.

cocktails.name: Black Russian
instructions: Fill an old fashioned glass with ice cubes.
Pour in the vodka and coffee liqueur.
Stir gently.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide credits Gustave Tops, a bartender at the Metropolitan Hotel in Brussels, with creating the Black Russian in 1949. He made it for Perle Mesta, the wealthy American socialite who served as US ambassador to Luxembourg from 1949 to 1953 and who appeared on the cover of TIME that year.

Mesta was famous for her lavish parties and was known as the "hostess with the mostest". She also inspired Irving Berlin's musical Call Me Madam. A float of cream turns the drink into a White Russian, and topping it with cream and cola makes a Colorado Bulldog.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Short, dark and simple. The coffee liqueur gives roasted coffee, light vanilla and a syrupy sweetness, while the vodka adds strength without much flavour of its own, so the result tastes like a strong, sweetened iced coffee. Served over ice, it gradually dilutes and softens. It is smooth and dessert-like but noticeably more alcoholic than it tastes.

cocktails.name: Bloody Mary
instructions: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir gently.
Pour into a rocks glass (or a highball over ice if requested).
Garnish with celery and, optionally, a lemon wedge.
cocktails.history:
The Bloody Mary is often credited to Fernand "Pete" Petiot, said to have created it in the early 1920s at Harry's New York Bar in Paris. Research by Jack McGarry, published by Difford's Guide, suggests Petiot instead spiced up an existing vodka and tomato mix while working at the St. Regis Hotel in New York.

That research names the Hollywood entertainer George Jessel as the more likely originator of the basic pairing, and possibly of the name. A 1939 drink credited to Jessel resembles today's recipe. Several stories explain the name, and the St. Regis has its own version of the drink's origin.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Savoury, spicy and full-bodied. Tomato juice provides a thick, umami-rich base, lemon lifts it with acidity, and Worcestershire sauce adds deep, salty and tangy notes. Hot sauce, celery salt and pepper can be adjusted from mild to fiery. The vodka sits quietly underneath, adding strength rather than flavour, which makes this the classic brunch and hair-of-the-dog drink.

sources.title: The history of the Bloody Mary

cocktails.name: Boulevardier
instructions: Pour all ingredients into a mixing glass with ice cubes.
Stir well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
Garnish with an orange zest, or optionally a lemon zest.
cocktails.history:
The Boulevardier first appears in Harry MacElhone's 1927 book Barflies and Cocktails. It is not in the main recipe list but in a chapter by Arthur Moss, a Paris newspaper columnist. Moss belonged to a group of wealthy American expatriates who called themselves boulevardiers because they roamed between Harry's New York Bar and other Paris nightspots.

Moss credited the drink to Erskine Gwynne, a nephew of the railroad tycoon Alfred Vanderbilt. Gwynne co-founded the Paris magazine Boulevardier, modelled on The New Yorker, which launched the same year as the book, hence the drink's name. The original recipe was equal parts Campari, Italian vermouth and bourbon.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A richer, warmer cousin of the Negroni. Bourbon or rye replaces gin, bringing vanilla, caramel and baking spice, or a drier peppery edge with rye. Campari adds bitter orange and a firm bitterness, and sweet vermouth ties everything together with dark fruit and herbal sweetness. Served cold and stirred, it is silky, bittersweet and warming, with an expressive orange-oil aroma.

cocktails.name: Bramble
instructions: Shake the gin, lemon juice and sugar syrup with ice.
Strain into a chilled old fashioned glass filled with crushed ice.
Drizzle the crème de mûre over the top in a circular motion.
Optionally garnish with a lemon slice and blackberries.
cocktails.history:
Dick Bradsell, one of the most influential London bartenders of his generation, created the Bramble in the mid-1980s at Fred's Club in Soho. In accounts he wrote in 2001 and 2015, republished by Difford's Guide, he described the drink as essentially a gin sour with blackberry added.

The drink is served over crushed ice, with blackberry liqueur poured over the top so it bleeds down through the glass. Difford's ranks it among the best and most popular drinks to come out of the 1980s, and it is now a modern classic in British bars.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Tart, juicy and refreshing. The base is a well-balanced gin sour with bright lemon and a clean juniper backbone, and crushed ice keeps it very cold. Crème de mûre bleeds down through the ice, adding dark berry sweetness and a purple streak. The first sips are fruitier, and the drink becomes more evenly blended and sour as the ice melts.

cocktails.name: Caipirinha
instructions: Place the lime wedges and sugar in a double old fashioned glass and muddle gently.
Fill the glass with cracked ice.
Add the cachaça and stir gently to combine.
cocktails.history:
The Caipirinha has no single known inventor. PUNCH describes it emerging in the mid-19th century among the caipiras, rural people of the countryside near Brazil's Atlantic rainforest, who drank this cheap mix of lime, sugar and cane spirit. Difford's Guide translates the name as "country little girl" and links it to rural São Paulo state.

One story ties it to a cachaça, lime, honey and garlic remedy drunk during the Spanish flu. Citing historian David Wondrich, PUNCH notes it was once called the Batida Paulista, appeared in travel accounts in the 1940s, and became popular abroad in the late 1970s and early 1980s.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rustic, zesty and powerful. Muddled lime releases both juice and aromatic peel oils, giving sharp acidity and a slightly bitter citrus edge, while the sugar rounds it out. Cachaça adds a grassy, vegetal sugarcane character that sets it apart from rum-based sours. Served over plenty of ice, it starts bold and becomes more mellow and refreshing as it dilutes.

sources.title: The Caipirinha Has Been Here All Along

cocktails.name: Clover Club
instructions: Pour all ingredients into a cocktail shaker.
Shake well with ice.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
Garnish with fresh raspberries.
cocktails.history:
The drink takes its name from the Clover Club, a club founded in January 1882 by a group of prominent Philadelphia journalists. From 1883 until 1897 its members met every Thursday at the city's Hotel Bellevue, and over time the membership grew to include lawyers, bankers and leading businessmen.

The earliest known reference, found by historian David Wondrich, is a 1901 New York Press article. In it, a wine steward at the Waldorf-Astoria gave a recipe of egg white, lemon, raspberry syrup and Plymouth gin. Recipes appeared in cocktail books from 1909. In 1911 a newspaper described it as fashionable in New York, especially with women, and said it came from Philadelphia.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Silky, pink and gently tart. Raspberry syrup gives bright red-berry sweetness, and lemon adds acidity that keeps the fruit from becoming cloying. Egg white makes a soft, foamy head and a smooth, rounded texture, while gin keeps a dry juniper backbone. It is elegant and fruity but balanced, finishing clean rather than sugary.

cocktails.name: Cosmopolitan
instructions: Add all ingredients to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a large cocktail glass.
Garnish with a lemon twist.
cocktails.history:
Several bartenders have a claim to the Cosmopolitan. Drawing on research by Miss Charming, Difford's Guide reports that Neal Murray mixed a pink combination of a Cape Codder and a Kamikaze in Minnesota in 1975. He later spread it in San Francisco, where the drink circulated during the late 1970s and 1980s.

Separately, Cheryl Cook has a well-supported claim to a version made with the new Absolut Citron at The Strand in Miami in the late 1980s. In New York, Melissa Huffsmith and Toby Cecchini upgraded it with fresh lime and Cointreau at The Odeon. Dale DeGroff later helped popularise it.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Tart, fruity and crisp. Citrus vodka and Cointreau give bright lemon and orange notes, fresh lime adds a sharp, refreshing acidity, and cranberry juice contributes a light, dry berry flavour and the signature pale pink colour. It is cleaner and less sweet than its reputation suggests, with a light body and a zesty finish lifted by the lemon twist.

cocktails.name: Cuba Libre
instructions: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Build the rum, lime juice and cola in the glass.
Garnish with a lime wedge.
cocktails.history:
The most widely told story, which Difford's Guide notes follows Bacardi's account, places the Cuba Libre in Havana around 1900. American soldiers were stationed in Cuba after the war with Spain, and Coca-Cola had recently reached the island. A Captain Russell of the US Signal Corps is said to have ordered rum and cola with lime in a Havana bar. His toast to a free Cuba, "Por Cuba libre", gave the drink its name.

The story rests on a sworn statement made in 1964 by a witness, Fausto Rodriguez. The drink was hugely popular in America in the 1940s, helped by the Andrews Sisters' 1945 hit "Rum and Coca-Cola" and by wartime shortages of whiskey and gin, which pushed drinkers toward Caribbean rum.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Easy, refreshing and familiar. Cola provides sweetness, caramel and spice, and white rum adds a light, clean sugarcane warmth without dominating. The squeeze of lime is what turns a simple rum and cola into a Cuba Libre, cutting the sweetness with acidity and adding fresh citrus aroma. It is long, fizzy and very cold, ideal for casual drinking.

cocktails.name: Daiquiri
instructions: Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker and stir to dissolve the sugar.
Add ice and shake.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
The Daiquiri is credited to Jennings Stockton Cox, an American mining engineer working near the small town of Daiquirí in southeastern Cuba around 1898. Difford's Guide reports that he experimented with the local Bacardi rum, mixing it with limes and sugar. A fellow engineer, Francesco Pagliuchi, later wrote a letter in 1948 backing Cox's claim.

The drink is closely related to the older Cuban Canchanchara. US Admiral Lucius Johnson tasted it with Cox in 1909 and brought it to the Army & Navy Club in Washington. Its first appearance in a recipe book was Jacques Straub's 1914 Drinks.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Crisp, clean and perfectly simple. Light rum provides a gentle sugarcane sweetness and subtle vanilla, fresh lime brings vivid, mouth-watering sourness, and fine sugar rounds off the edges. Shaken hard and served very cold, it is bright and refreshing, with sweet and sour in close balance and no single flavour dominating. It is a benchmark for how good a three-ingredient sour can be.

cocktails.name: Dark 'n' Stormy
instructions: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the ginger beer.
Float the rum on top.
Garnish with a lime wedge or slice.
cocktails.history: The Dark 'n' Stormy is regarded as the national drink of Bermuda, which produces both ginger beer and Gosling's rum, the dark rum most associated with it. Difford's Guide says nobody knows who first mixed or named it. Legend has it that British sailors on shore leave in Bermuda after the First World War created it, or at least enjoyed it first. Difford's places it in the Mule family of spirit and ginger drinks, and the IBA recipe names Gosling's rum.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bold and spicy. Dark rum brings molasses, caramel and dried-fruit richness, floating in a dark layer at first before it mixes in. Ginger beer adds sweetness, plenty of fizz and a peppery ginger heat that builds with each sip. A squeeze of the lime garnish adds welcome acidity. The drink is long and refreshing yet full-flavoured, with a warming finish.

cocktails.name: Dry Martini
cocktails.garnish: Lemon peel oils expressed over the drink, or green olives on request
instructions: Pour the gin and dry vermouth into a mixing glass with ice cubes.
Stir well.
Strain into a chilled martini glass.
Express lemon peel oils over the drink, or garnish with green olives if requested.
cocktails.history:
Nobody knows exactly where the Martini began. Difford's Guide reports the widely accepted theory that it evolved from the Martinez, itself a descendant of the Manhattan, during a period full of similar gin and vermouth drinks. Harry Johnson printed the first known "Martini" recipe in 1888, and it was sweet.

Over time the drink became drier. The first known recipe actually titled "Dry Martini Cocktail" appeared in a 1904 French book by Frank P. Newman, a bartender at the Ritz in Paris. It called for equal parts gin and dry vermouth with bitters. Ratios kept shifting toward less vermouth through the 20th century.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bracing, cold and elegant. Gin dominates, so juniper, citrus peel and other botanicals lead the palate, while the small measure of dry vermouth adds a subtle herbal, wine-like dryness and a silky texture. Stirring keeps it crystal clear and very cold. A twist of lemon adds a bright aromatic lift, while olives instead give a faintly briny, savoury edge.

cocktails.name: Espresso Martini
instructions: Pour all ingredients into a cocktail shaker.
Shake well with ice.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
Garnish with three coffee beans.
cocktails.history:
London bartender Dick Bradsell created the drink around 1983 at the Soho Brasserie on Old Compton Street, according to Difford's Guide. It was then called the Vodka Espresso and served on the rocks. A customer, said to be a model, asked for something that would wake her up and get her drunk. The coffee machine sat right beside Bradsell's station, and vodka was the fashionable spirit.

In 1997, while Bradsell was working at Match bar in Clerkenwell, a colleague served it straight up in a martini glass, during the 1990s craze for vodka "martinis". Bradsell adjusted the recipe, and in 1998 he renamed it the Pharmaceutical Stimulant for Damien Hirst's Pharmacy restaurant in Notting Hill.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, bittersweet and energising. Fresh espresso gives roasted, slightly bitter coffee flavour and, when shaken hot and hard, a creamy tan foam on top. Coffee liqueur adds sweetness and hints of vanilla and caramel, and a touch of sugar syrup balances the coffee's bitterness. Vodka provides clean strength. It is silky and dessert-like, but the finish is dry and coffee-forward.

cocktails.name: French 75
instructions: Shake the gin, lemon juice and sugar syrup with ice.
Strain into a Champagne flute.
Top up with Champagne.
Stir gently.
cocktails.history:
The French 75 is named after the French 75mm field gun, a symbol of hope during the First World War. Difford's Guide suggests a Paris bartender, probably Henry Tépé of Henry's Bar, named a "Soixante-Quinze" after it around 1914 or 1915. That first version mixed gin, apple brandy, grenadine and lemon and was served in a cocktail glass.

The gin, lemon, sugar and champagne version first appears in Judge Jr.'s 1927 book Here's How, served in a tall glass. Serving it in a champagne flute only became standard in the 1980s. Cognac versions arrived later, sometimes under the name French 125.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bright, elegant and celebratory. The gin sour base gives zesty lemon, a touch of sweetness and a clean juniper lift. Champagne adds fine bubbles, toasty, biscuity notes and crisp acidity that lengthen the drink. Despite its light, sparkling feel, it is stronger than it seems, a playful nod to the artillery piece it is named after.

cocktails.name: Gin Fizz

ingredients.note: For shaking only; served without ice

instructions: Shake the gin, lemon juice and simple syrup with ice.
Strain into a thin tall tumbler with no ice.
Top with a splash of soda water.
Garnish with a lemon slice and, optionally, a lemon zest.
cocktails.history:
The Gin Fizz is a mid-19th-century classic. Difford's Guide points to its appearance in the 1876 edition of Jerry Thomas's Bar-tenders Guide. There it is listed as a variation of the Whiskey Fizz: spirit, lemon and gum syrup shaken with ice, strained, and topped up with soda water from a siphon.

Difford's notes that a fizz is traditionally served in a smaller glass than a Collins, with no ice in the glass. Adding egg white makes a Silver Fizz, egg yolk a Golden Fizz, a whole egg a Royal Fizz, and sparkling wine a Diamond Fizz.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Clean, tart and effervescent. Fresh lemon leads with lively acidity, a little syrup takes off the sharp edge, and gin adds crisp juniper and botanical notes. The soda lengthens the drink and adds a light sparkle. Served without ice, it is meant to be drunk quickly while it is cold and fizzy. It is a simple, thirst-quenching sour.

cocktails.name: Gin Rickey
instructions: Pre-chill the glass.
Shake the gin, lime juice and sugar syrup with ice.
Strain into an ice-filled glass.
Top with soda water.
cocktails.history:
The Rickey family of drinks is believed to have been created around 1880 by bartender George A. Williamson at Shoemaker's bar in Washington, D.C. It is named after Colonel Joseph Kyle Rickey, a Democratic lobbyist who reportedly liked to squeeze fresh lime into his whiskey and lengthen it with soda. Rickey later bought Shoemaker's in 1883 and also became a major importer of limes into the United States.

The gin version appears in print in Harry Johnson's bartender's manual of 1900, which called for Old Tom or Holland gin. The Rickey differs from the Collins mainly in using lime instead of lemon, and it is traditionally served in a smaller glass. One reader note on Difford's Guide recalls that the Colonel preferred his Rickeys without sugar.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Sharp, dry and fizzy. London dry gin gives a crisp juniper and citrus-peel backbone, while fresh lime adds a bright, tart bite that dominates the drink. Only a touch of sugar softens the edges, so it stays much drier than a Collins or Gimlet. Lengthened with soda over ice, it feels light, clean and bracing, a simple, thirst-quenching highball with a zesty lime aroma.

cocktails.name: Hemingway Special

ingredients.note: IBA specifies 'rum'; El Floridita uses light Cuban rum

instructions: Pour all ingredients into a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a large cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
This Daiquiri variation comes from El Floridita in Havana. Difford's Guide credits its legendary head bartender, Constantino "Constante" Ribalaigua Vert, who made it for Ernest Hemingway. After trying the bar's standard frozen Daiquiri, Hemingway is said to have asked for it without sugar and with double the rum. Difford's links his dislike of sugar to a hereditary illness.

The drink was first called "Daiquiri like Papa" and then the Papa Doble. Later, head bartender Antonio Meilan added maraschino and grapefruit juice, and the drink took the name Hemingway Special. Hemingway kept a room in Havana in the 1930s.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Sharp, dry and citrus-driven. Without added sugar, it relies on maraschino for a subtle, nutty cherry sweetness, while grapefruit juice adds a bittersweet, slightly floral tartness alongside fresh lime. A generous pour of rum gives body and a clean cane note. It is noticeably more sour and spirit-forward than a standard Daiquiri, a drink for lovers of tart flavours.

cocktails.name: Irish Coffee

ingredients.note: At least one teaspoon; sugar syrup may be used instead

instructions: Pour warm black coffee into a preheated Irish coffee glass.
Add the whiskey and at least one teaspoon of sugar, and stir until dissolved.
Carefully pour the chilled cream over the back of a spoon held just above the coffee so it floats on top without mixing.
cocktails.history:
Difford's Guide credits Joe Sheridan, a chef turned bartender from County Tyrone, with creating the drink in late 1944 or early 1945 at the flying-boat port of Foynes in western Ireland. He added whiskey to hot coffee to warm American passengers arriving on a cold, wet evening. When they asked whether it was Brazilian coffee, he said it was Irish coffee.

The drink continued at nearby Shannon Airport, where travel writer Stanton Delaplane tried it. In 1952 he and Jack Koeppler of San Francisco's Buena Vista Café set out to recreate it. After much trial and error, including getting the cream to float, the Buena Vista made it famous in America.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Warming, comforting and layered. Hot black coffee and Irish whiskey make a robust, slightly sweet base with roasted, toasty and gently fruity notes. The cold cream floating on top gives a contrast in both temperature and texture: you sip the hot, boozy coffee through the cool, rich cream. Sugar balances the coffee's bitterness and helps the cream float.

cocktails.name: John Collins
instructions: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour all ingredients directly into the glass.
Stir gently.
Garnish with a lemon slice and a maraschino cherry.
cocktails.history:
The Collins appears to have developed from Gin Punch. Its creation and name are attributed to John (or possibly Jim) Collins, head waiter at Limmer's Hotel on Conduit Street in London during the 1800s. Limmer's coffee house was popular with sporting men and was already known for its Gin Punch in the early 1800s.

Difford's Guide suggests the drink may have become the Tom Collins when it was made with Old Tom gin. Harry Johnson's 1882 Bartenders' Manual lists a John Collins made with Dutch gin and a Tom Collins with Old Tom. The John Collins was first made with genever, then Old Tom, and finally London dry gin.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Tall, crisp and thirst-quenching. Think of it as sparkling gin lemonade: fresh lemon gives bright acidity, sugar syrup softens it, and gin adds dry juniper and botanical notes. Soda water lengthens the drink and keeps it lively, so it is light-bodied and very refreshing over plenty of ice. The cherry garnish adds a small touch of sweetness at the end.

cocktails.name: Kir
instructions: Pour the crème de cassis into a chilled glass.
Top up with chilled dry white wine.
cocktails.history:
According to Difford's Guide, the drink is said to date to 1904. That year a waiter named Faivre at the Café George in Dijon is said to have first mixed white wine with crème de cassis, and the drink was first called "Cassis Blanc".

It took its current name from Canon Félix Kir, a Catholic priest and French Resistance hero who became mayor of Dijon in 1945. He served the local cassis and Bourgogne Aligoté wine at official receptions to promote regional products. In 1951 he gave a cassis producer the right to use his name, and "Kir" was registered as a brand the following year.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Light, fruity and refreshing. A crisp, acidic dry white wine forms the base, and a small measure of crème de cassis adds ripe blackcurrant sweetness and a pretty ruby-pink colour. When the proportions are right, the wine's acidity balances the rich liqueur, so the drink is gently sweet rather than syrupy. It is a low-alcohol, easy French aperitif to serve well chilled.

cocktails.name: Last Word
instructions: Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker.
Shake with ice.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
The earliest known mention of the Last Word is in a souvenir menu sent to Detroit Athletic Club members with the club's July-August 1916 magazine. It lists only the name and the price, which was twice that of a Manhattan. Ted Saucier's 1951 book Bottoms Up! confirms the link to the club and gives an equal-parts recipe.

Saucier credits the vaudeville performer Frank Fogarty, known as the "Dublin Minstrel", with bringing the drink to New York. Fogarty usually ended his act with a recitation, which some think explains the name. The club put the drink back on its menu in 2009.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Intense, herbal and finely balanced. Green Chartreuse brings a powerful mix of alpine herbs, mint and spice, while maraschino adds a dry, funky cherry-almond sweetness. Fresh lime cuts through both with sharp acidity, and gin adds a juniper backbone. Equal parts produce a pale green drink that is sweet, sour and herbal at once, with a long, complex finish.

cocktails.name: Long Island Iced Tea
instructions: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the vodka, tequila, rum, gin, Cointreau, lemon juice and simple syrup.
Top with cola.
Stir gently and garnish with a lemon slice if desired.
cocktails.history:
Of the many origin stories, Difford's Guide considers this the most credible: Robert "Rosebud" Butt created the drink in the 1970s, perhaps in 1972, at the Oak Beach Inn in Babylon, on New York's Long Island. The name comes from that location and from the way the cola-topped drink looks like iced tea.

Because it disguises how much alcohol it contains, some people claim it dates back to Prohibition. Its popularity peaked in the early 1980s. In 1985 The New York Times reported that the drink was sweeping bars on Long Island and across the country.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Deceptively easy-drinking and very strong. Five spirits combine into a fairly neutral, boozy base, with the tequila and gin adding faint earthy and botanical notes. Lemon and sugar syrup create a sweet-and-sour, lemonade-like body, Cointreau adds orange, and a splash of cola gives the tea colour and a hint of caramel. It drinks like spiked iced tea but packs a punch.

cocktails.name: Mai Tai

ingredients.note: 30 ml amber Jamaican rum + 30 ml Martinique molasses rum (not rhum agricole)

cocktails.garnish: Pineapple spear, mint leaves and lime peel
instructions: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a double rocks (old fashioned) or highball glass.
cocktails.history:
Victor Bergeron, better known as Trader Vic, said he came up with the Mai Tai in 1944 at his restaurant in Oakland, California, which he had opened a decade earlier. He served the new mix to two friends visiting from Tahiti, and one of them reportedly reacted with a Tahitian phrase meaning roughly 'out of this world', which gave the drink its name. His original build leaned on a 17-year-old Jamaican rum, lime, orange curaçao, rich sugar syrup and French orgeat.

The story is not uncontested. Ernest Raymond Beaumont-Gantt, owner of Don the Beachcomber's in Hollywood, also claimed the drink, and some accounts even place its birth in Tahiti; Bergeron firmly rejected both claims in his 1972 writing. The cocktail spread from California to Hawaii in the 1950s, when Bergeron set it up for Matson Line hotel bars, and it went on to become the emblem of the tiki movement.
cocktails.tasteProfile: A rich, rum-forward sour with real depth. Aged rums bring molasses, toffee and funky fruit notes, sharp lime cuts through, and orange curaçao adds bittersweet citrus peel. Orgeat gives a soft, nutty almond sweetness and a slightly creamy texture that rounds everything off. Served over plenty of ice with fragrant mint on top, it tastes tropical without being sugary, balancing boozy warmth against bright acidity.

cocktails.name: Manhattan
instructions: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice cubes.
Stir well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
The Manhattan surfaced in New York in the 1860s or 1870s and is often called the first 'modern' cocktail, because it brought sweet vermouth into an Old Fashioned-style whiskey drink. A New York newspaper letter of 1882 described the whiskey, vermouth and bitters mix as newly fashionable, and full recipes appeared in several bar books in 1884.

A long-repeated legend places its invention at an 1874 Manhattan Club banquet for Samuel Tilden, sometimes linked to Lady Randolph Churchill, but historians have shown she was in England giving birth to Winston at the time. Difford's Guide considers the most plausible account the one given by Hoffman House bartender William Mulhall in 1923, which points to a bar owner named Black; research suggests George Black, who ran the Manhattan Inn on Broadway.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Spirit-forward, smooth and gently sweet. Rye whiskey gives a spicy, slightly dry backbone with notes of grain, pepper and oak, while sweet vermouth adds dark fruit, herbs and a soft wine richness. A dash of Angostura ties them together with warm baking spice and a faint bitter edge. Stirred and served very cold, it feels silky and weighty, finishing with a hint of cherry from the garnish.

cocktails.name: Margarita
instructions: Optionally rim half of a chilled cocktail glass with salt.
Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into the chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
The Margarita is widely seen as a tequila version of the Daisy, an old family of spirit, citrus and liqueur drinks; 'margarita' is Spanish for daisy. A Tequila Daisy was being promoted in a Tijuana-area saloon by 1936, the 1937 Café Royal Cocktail Book printed a near-identical 'Picador', and a 1939 Tequila Sour with Cointreau, lime and a salted rim came close to the modern drink.

The name 'Margarita' first appears in print in 1953. Many people have claimed to have invented or named it, including Danny Negrete, Francisco 'Pancho' Morales in Ciudad Juárez, Carlos 'Danny' Herrera at Rancho La Gloria and the socialite Margaret Sames in Acapulco. None of these claims has been proven. A José Cuervo promotional push by distributor Young's Market from 1955 helped make the drink famous across the United States.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bright, tart and refreshing with an agave core. Tequila brings earthy, vegetal and peppery notes, fresh lime supplies a sharp sour snap, and triple sec adds sweet orange that softens the edges. The optional salt rim lifts the citrus and tames any bitterness, making each sip pop. Served cold and straight up, it is clean, zesty and lively, with a slightly dry, lingering finish.

cocktails.name: Mimosa
instructions: Pour the orange juice into a flute.
Gently pour in the Prosecco.
Stir gently.
cocktails.history:
The Mimosa is often credited to Frank Meier, the bartender at the Ritz Hotel in Paris, with dates given as either the early 1920s or 1925. Meier's 1936 book is the first known publication to list it, calling it the 'Mimosa or Champagne Orange' and serving it over ice in a large wineglass. Oddly, the book does not mark it with the symbol Meier used for his own creations, so his authorship is uncertain.

Its close cousin, the Buck's Fizz, is believed to have been created around 1921 at Buck's Club in London and appears in print earlier, in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book. The two are nearly the same mix of orange juice and sparkling wine; traditionally the Buck's Fizz uses more wine, while the Mimosa was the version served with ice. The IBA notes the two names are used interchangeably.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Light, fruity and gently fizzy. Fresh orange juice provides sweet, juicy citrus with a little tang, while dry Prosecco adds crisp bubbles, a touch of green apple and pear, and a refreshing lift. Equal parts keep it low in alcohol and easy to drink, more like sparkling juice than a strong cocktail. The result is bright, breezy and soft, a natural fit for brunch.

sources.title: Buck's Fizz & Mimosa cocktails – history & recipes

cocktails.name: Mint Julep
instructions: Gently muddle the mint with the sugar and water in a julep cup.
Fill the cup with cracked ice.
Add the bourbon and stir until the cup is well frosted.
cocktails.history:
The word 'julep' goes back to the Persian 'gulab', a rosewater syrup, which passed into Arabic and Latin and was later used in Europe for herbal medicinal syrups. The earliest verified reference to the American drink comes from John Davis's 1803 account of his travels, describing Virginians taking a morning dram of spirit steeped with mint. At that point juleps could be based on rum, brandy or whiskey.

Jerry Thomas's 1862 guide offered cognac, gin and whiskey versions, and by about 1900 whiskey had become the usual base. The bourbon julep is now tied to the Kentucky Derby at Churchill Downs: it became the race's official drink in 1938, and from 1939 the track commissioned souvenir glasses after many of its glasses were taken home. Around 120,000 are sold over the race weekend.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Cold, aromatic and strong. A heap of crushed ice chills and slowly dilutes the bourbon, whose caramel, vanilla and oak notes come through softly. Fresh mint adds a cool, green perfume that hits the nose before each sip, and a little sugar smooths the spirit's heat. It is simple and sweet-edged rather than sour, with the frosty cup making it feel especially refreshing on a hot day.

cocktails.name: Mojito
instructions: Muddle the mint with the sugar and lime juice in the glass.
Add a splash of soda water and fill the glass with ice.
Pour in the rum and top with soda water.
Stir gently to combine.
cocktails.history:
The Mojito's exact origins are unclear. One popular theory links it to the Draque, a medicinal mix of crude cane spirit, sugar, lime and mint said to be named after Sir Francis Drake, who menaced Havana in 1586. Once rum replaced the rough cane spirit in the 1800s, the drink is said to have taken the Mojito name, possibly with encouragement from Bacardi. Another theory points to American visitors bringing the Mint Julep to Cuba.

The earliest known recipe, a 'Mojo Criollo', appears in a Cuban book from 1927, and the name 'Mojito' turns up on a Sloppy Joe's Bar menu in 1931–32. The famous link to Hemingway and La Bodeguita del Medio in Havana rests on a framed note in the bar, but nothing in Hemingway's known writing mentions the drink.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Fresh, minty and thirst-quenching. Light white rum keeps things clean and gently sweet, while lime juice brings a sharp, zesty tang. Muddled mint releases a cool herbal fragrance that runs through every sip, and the sugar balances the sourness without making it heavy. Topped with soda and lots of ice, it is long, bubbly and light, tasting more like a herbal limeade with a rum backbone.

cocktails.name: Moscow Mule
cocktails.glass: Copper Mule Mug Or Rocks Glass
instructions: Combine the vodka and ginger beer in a mule cup or rocks glass with ice.
Add the lime juice.
Stir gently.
cocktails.history:
The Moscow Mule appeared sometime between 1941 and 1946, though where and when exactly is disputed. In 1939 John G. Martin had acquired the Smirnoff vodka rights for Heublein, while his friend Jack Morgan, owner of the Cock 'n' Bull pub on Hollywood's Sunset Strip, was struggling to sell his own ginger beer. One legend has the pair combining their slow-selling products, with a squeeze of lime, during a meeting in New York.

A rival version, reported in a 2007 Wall Street Journal article, credits Cock 'n' Bull head bartender Wes Price, who supposedly invented it to clear surplus ginger beer. The engraved copper mug, linked to a friend of Morgan's who had inherited a copper business, became the drink's trademark, and Martin promoted it by photographing bartenders with Smirnoff and the mug using an early Polaroid camera.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Crisp, spicy and refreshing. Vodka stays neutral in the background, letting the ginger beer take the lead with its peppery heat, gentle sweetness and lively fizz. A splash of fresh lime adds a bright, tart edge that keeps the drink from tasting sugary. Served over ice, traditionally in a chilled copper mug, it feels cold, zesty and easygoing, with a warming ginger tingle on the finish.

cocktails.name: Negroni
instructions: Pour all ingredients directly into a chilled old fashioned glass filled with ice.
Stir gently.
cocktails.history:
The usual story places the Negroni in Florence around 1919. Count Camillo Negroni, a regular at the Casoni bar, is said to have asked for a stronger Americano, and bartender Fosco Scarselli swapped the soda water for gin. Other customers began ordering 'the Count's drink', and the name stuck. The Americano itself descends from the Milano-Torino, a mix of Milanese Campari and Turin vermouth.

The tale has its doubters. A descendant of the Negroni family has questioned whether Camillo was ever a count and has promoted a French general, Pascal Olivier de Negroni, as the true inventor. Equal-parts gin, Campari and vermouth also appears as the 'Campari Mixte' in a 1929 French cocktail book, while the earliest recipes under the Negroni name date only from the late 1940s and 1950s.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bold, bittersweet and aromatic. Campari leads with bitter orange, rhubarb and gentian, while sweet vermouth adds plummy fruit, vanilla and herbal sweetness. Gin's juniper and botanicals give structure and a dry, piney lift. Equal parts keep the three in tension, so the drink feels rich and slightly syrupy at first, then finishes long, dry and pleasantly bitter. Orange on the side brightens the aroma.

cocktails.name: Old Fashioned

ingredients.note: a few dashes of plain water

cocktails.garnish: Orange slice or zest and a cocktail cherry
instructions: Place the sugar cube in an old fashioned glass and saturate it with bitters.
Add a few dashes of plain water and muddle until the sugar dissolves.
Fill the glass with ice and add the whiskey.
Stir gently.
cocktails.history:
The Old Fashioned is a direct descendant of the earliest definition of a 'cock-tail', printed in 1806 as spirit, sugar, water and bitters. Aromatic bitters date back to a London apothecary around 1690, and by the late 1700s Americans were mixing them with whiskey to make the Whiskey Cocktail, served without ice. During the 1800s bartenders dressed it up into 'Fancy' and 'Improved' versions with absinthe, curaçao and other liqueurs.

Drinkers who wanted the plain original began asking for an 'Old-Fashioned' Whiskey Cocktail, and the name stuck along with the heavy tumbler now called an old fashioned glass. During Prohibition, muddled orange and cherry crept in, possibly to hide rough spirit. The cocktail revivals in London in the 1990s and later in the US brought back the simpler, unfruited style.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, mellow and whiskey-led. The bourbon or rye shows caramel, vanilla, oak and spice, softened by a little dissolved sugar that rounds out the alcohol. Angostura adds warm clove and cinnamon notes plus a faint bitterness, and the dilution from stirring over ice opens up the spirit. The citrus garnish brings a fresh orange-oil aroma, so the drink feels both comforting and quietly complex.

cocktails.name: Paloma
instructions: Pour the tequila into a highball glass and squeeze in the lime juice.
Add ice and a pinch of salt.
Top with pink grapefruit soda.
Stir gently.
cocktails.history:
Despite being one of Mexico's favourite tequila drinks, the Paloma has a surprisingly thin paper trail. It almost certainly depends on grapefruit soda: Squirt was created in Arizona in 1938 and began reaching Mexico in the 1950s, and historian David Wondrich suggests the drink took shape around then. However, researchers have not found the Paloma name in print until the late 1990s, with a 1999 trade publication and a 2000 cocktail book among the earliest references.

Two popular origin stories have been challenged. A widely quoted 1953 pamphlet by 'Evan Harrison' appears to have been an invention added to Wikipedia as a joke, and Don Javier of La Capilla bar in the town of Tequila, often named as the creator, reportedly denied inventing it. The name means 'dove' in Spanish.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Zesty, salty and easy-drinking. Agave tequila provides an earthy, peppery base, while pink grapefruit soda brings sweet-tart citrus with a pleasantly bitter pith note and plenty of fizz. A squeeze of lime sharpens it, and a pinch of salt makes the grapefruit taste brighter and juicier. Long, cold and lightly sweet, it is a more casual and refreshing alternative to the Margarita.

sources.title: Paloma History – Tracing the Facts and Fiction about this Tequila Cocktail's History

cocktails.name: Penicillin
instructions: Muddle the fresh ginger in a shaker.
Add the remaining ingredients except the Islay single malt.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake.
Fine-strain into a chilled old fashioned glass with ice.
Float the Islay single malt on top.
cocktails.history:
Sam Ross created the Penicillin in 2005 at Milk & Honey, the influential New York bar. Starting from the Gold Rush, a bourbon, lemon and honey sour already popular at the bar, he switched to blended Scotch, added honey and ginger syrup, and finished the drink with a float of smoky Islay single malt. His original was garnished with crystallised ginger.

The drink travelled quickly through the Milk & Honey family of bars and on to cocktail bars in the US and London, becoming one of the best-known modern classics of the 21st-century cocktail revival. It was later added to the IBA's official list in the New Era category. Its name plays on the idea of a soothing, medicinal-sounding mix of honey, lemon and ginger.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Warming, spicy and gently smoky. The blended Scotch base gives malt and honeyed grain, lifted by fresh lemon's sour brightness and smoothed by rich honey. Fresh ginger adds a peppery bite that tingles on the tongue. The float of Islay whisky lands first on the nose, wrapping the drink in peat smoke and sea-spray notes, while the body underneath stays balanced, soothing and lightly sweet.

cocktails.name: Piña Colada

ingredients.note: fresh; 4 slices of fresh pineapple can be used instead

instructions: Blend all ingredients with ice in an electric blender.
Pour into a large glass.
Serve with straws.
cocktails.history:
Puerto Rico regards the Piña Colada as its national drink, but three bartenders have claimed it. Ramón 'Monchito' Marrero said he first made it at the Caribe Hilton's Beachcomber Bar in San Juan in 1952, while the hotel itself gives 1954; he used the then-new Coco López cream of coconut. Ricardo Garcia, another Caribe Hilton bartender, also claimed it, and Ramón Portas Mingot said he created it in 1963 at Barrachina in Old San Juan.

Difford's Guide suggests all three may have played a part, with the Caribe Hilton the most likely birthplace. The name, meaning 'strained pineapple', is older: a 1922 Travel magazine piece describes a Cuban Piña Colada of rum, pineapple, lime and sugar with no coconut. The modern drink only reached cocktail books in the late 1960s.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Creamy, sweet and tropical. Coconut cream gives a lush, velvety texture and toasted-coconut richness, while pineapple juice adds juicy, tangy fruit that keeps it from feeling too heavy. Light rum sits quietly underneath, adding gentle warmth and a hint of sugarcane. Blended with ice into a frosty, smooth slush, it tastes like a holiday dessert in a glass, with a mellow, fruity finish.

cocktails.name: Pisco Sour
cocktails.garnish: A few dashes of Amargo bitters on the foam
instructions: Shake all ingredients with ice.
Strain into a chilled goblet.
Add a few dashes of Amargo bitters on top of the foam.
cocktails.history:
The Pisco Sour has long been credited to Victor Morris, an American from Salt Lake City who moved to Peru in 1903 to work for a railway company. Family lore says he swapped whiskey for pisco when supplies ran short at a railway celebration. On 1 April 1916 he opened Morris' Bar in Lima, where his Pisco Sours became famous; a Peruvian magazine credited 'Mister Morris' with the drink in 1921.

After the bar closed in 1929, former staff carried the recipe to Lima's Hotel Bolívar and Country Club, and Mario Bruijet is sometimes credited with adding the bitters. However, a 1903 Lima cookbook already contains a pisco, lime, sugar and egg-white 'cocktail', suggesting the drink predates Morris. Peru and Chile both claim it, though Difford's Guide concludes it is Peruvian.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Silky, tart and aromatic. Pisco brings a fragrant, grapey and slightly floral spirit character, cut by bright lemon and softened by sugar syrup. Shaking with egg white creates a thick, velvety foam that makes the drink feel smooth and almost creamy. The drops of Amargo bitters on top add a warm, spicy perfume with every sip, balancing the fresh sourness with a gentle bitter edge.

cocktails.name: Ramos Gin Fizz
instructions: Add all ingredients except the soda water to a shaker with ice and shake for two minutes.
Double-strain, return the liquid to the shaker and shake hard without ice for one minute.
Strain into a highball glass.
Top with soda water.
cocktails.history:
Henry Charles Ramos created this drink in 1888 at the Imperial Cabinet Saloon on the corner of Gravier and Carondelet Streets in New Orleans, first calling it the New Orleans Fizz. It needed so much shaking that his bar reportedly employed teams of 'shaker boys' passing shakers down the line, and at the 1915 Mardi Gras even dozens of them reportedly struggled to keep up. In 1907 Ramos moved to the larger Stag Saloon.

When Prohibition arrived in 1919, Ramos closed his bar and the recipe stayed secret until a newspaper published it shortly after his death in 1928. Whether vanilla belonged in the original is still argued over. In 1935 the Roosevelt Hotel, now the Fairmont, bought the rights to the name, and Louisiana governor Huey P. Long famously had one of its bartenders train staff in New York.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Light, frothy and cloud-like. Long shaking whips cream and egg white into a tall, airy foam that rises above the glass, giving a texture somewhere between a milkshake and a soufflé. Underneath, gin's botanicals meet a lively mix of lemon and lime, sweetened just enough to taste like citrus meringue. Orange flower water adds a delicate floral perfume, and soda keeps the whole thing surprisingly fresh and bright.

cocktails.name: Rusty Nail
instructions: Pour both ingredients directly into an old fashioned glass filled with ice.
Stir gently.
cocktails.history:
Scotch and Drambuie make an obvious pairing, and the Rusty Nail's exact birth is hazy. Drambuie, a whisky liqueur sweetened with honey and spices, was first produced commercially in Edinburgh in 1908, so the combination may have been tried long before anyone recorded it. Cocktail historian David Wondrich traced the mix back to 1937, when a drink called the B.I.F. was made for the British Industries Fair.

Other accounts say the drink was created at a bar in Hawaii in 1942 for the artist Theodore Anderson. What is clearer is that it became fashionable in the 1950s at New York's 21 Club, and its two-ingredient simplicity has kept it on back bars ever since. Proportions vary widely according to taste.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Smooth, sweet and warming. Scotch whisky provides malt, oak and a touch of smoke, while Drambuie adds honey, heather, herbal spice and a rich liqueur sweetness. Stirred over ice, the two blend into a mellow, rounded sipper with a soft, syrupy texture. A twist of lemon zest lifts the aroma and keeps the sweetness from feeling cloying, leaving a long, honeyed finish.

cocktails.name: Sazerac

ingredients.note: used to rinse the glass; excess discarded
crushed ice to chill the glass; ice for stirring

instructions: Rinse a chilled old fashioned glass with the absinthe, add crushed ice and set aside.
Stir the cognac, sugar cube and Peychaud's bitters over ice in a mixing glass.
Discard the ice and excess absinthe from the prepared glass.
Strain the drink into the glass.
cocktails.history:
The Sazerac grew out of New Orleans' brandy cocktail culture. Pharmacist Antoine Amédée Peychaud, who arrived in the city as a refugee in 1795, created the bitters that still define the drink. Around the 1850s Sewell T. Taylor became local agent for Sazerac de Forge et Fils cognac, and a cocktail of that cognac, Peychaud's bitters and sugar became the house drink at the Exchange Coffee House, later renamed the Sazerac Coffee House.

When phylloxera devastated French vineyards from the late 1860s, Thomas Handy, who took over the bar and the bitters, is said to have switched to American rye whiskey, and an absinthe rinse was added around this time. Historian David Wondrich has questioned this traditional account, suggesting it began as a bottled whiskey cocktail. In 2008 it was named the official cocktail of New Orleans.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Bold, aromatic and layered. The cognac base offers dried fruit, vanilla and a soft, rounded warmth, sweetened lightly by the dissolved sugar cube. Peychaud's bitters bring bright anise, cherry and floral notes along with their signature red tint. The absinthe rinse leaves a haunting licorice and herbal aroma that hits before the first sip, and the lemon oil adds a fresh citrus lift over a long, dry finish.

cocktails.name: Sidecar
instructions: Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
The Sidecar emerged around the end of the First World War, and its creator is uncertain. David Embury wrote in 1948 that a friend invented it at a Paris bistro during the war, naming it after the motorcycle sidecar that carried a captain there; many assume he meant Harry's New York Bar. Yet the first printed recipe, in Robert Vermeire's 1922 book, credits Pat MacGarry, bartender at Buck's Club in London.

Harry MacElhone's own book from the same year also first credited MacGarry, though later editions seem to claim the drink for himself. Difford's Guide's best reading is that MacGarry created it in London and MacElhone popularised it in Paris. Early recipes used equal parts brandy, triple sec and lemon; the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book doubled the brandy, and the sugared rim came later.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Elegant, tart and warming. Cognac gives a rich base of dried fruit, vanilla and oak, while triple sec adds sweet orange peel and a little extra body. Fresh lemon juice cuts through with a crisp sourness that keeps the drink lively. Served very cold and straight up, it balances brandy depth with citrus brightness, finishing dry and slightly bittersweet, like a refined brandy-based relative of the Daiquiri.

cocktails.name: Spritz

ingredients.note: Campari, Cynar or Select are used in other versions

instructions: Build all ingredients into a wine glass filled with ice.
Stir gently.
cocktails.history:
The Spritz traces back to the Veneto in north-eastern Italy, which was part of the Austrian Empire in the 1800s. Austrian soldiers stationed there found the local wines strong and often diluted them with water, giving rise to the white wine and soda Spritzer. The name is linked to the German verb 'spritzen', meaning to splash or spray, and in Venetian dialect it is pronounced 'spriss'.

In time, Venetians added local bitter liqueurs such as Aperol, Campari, Select or Cynar, creating the Spritz al Bitter, also called the Spritz Veneziano. Gruppo Campari estimates that around 300,000 are drunk every day in the Veneto alone. The drink's international boom came much later, with the Aperol version becoming a worldwide favourite in the 2010s.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Light, bubbly and bittersweet. Aperol brings bright orange and rhubarb flavours with a gentle bitterness and a vivid orange colour, while Prosecco adds crisp fruit and lively fizz. A splash of soda stretches it into a long, low-alcohol drink, and plenty of ice keeps it cool. Easy and refreshing, it balances sweetness against a soft bitter finish, ideal as an early-evening aperitivo.

cocktails.name: Stinger
instructions: Add both ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
The Stinger's roots lie in 1890s New York. According to PUNCH, a shaken mix of cognac and crème de menthe was served around 1890 at a hotel by Madison Square Park as the Bartholdi Cocktail; at the Holland House, George Kappeler added Angostura and called it the Brant. The Stinger name appears around 1910 in a handwritten addition to William Boothby's American Bartender, credited to a San Francisco bar.

Jacques Straub printed it in his 1913 bartender's manual, and the drink became a society favourite in the 1920s thanks largely to Reginald Vanderbilt, who mixed them for friends at his New York mansion. It remained a popular after-dinner order through the 1940s and has been revived by several New York bars in recent years.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Cool, smooth and boozy. Cognac provides warmth, dried fruit and a mellow oak depth, while white crème de menthe adds a clean, sweet peppermint flavour that cools the palate. Stirred and served very cold, the two combine into a silky, spirit-forward drink that tastes like a grown-up after-dinner mint. It is sweet but not cloying, with a fresh, minty finish over the brandy's lingering warmth.

sources.title: The Stinger: cocktail history and New York recipes

cocktails.name: Tom Collins
cocktails.garnish: Orange wheel and maraschino cherry on a skewer
instructions: Pre-chill a Collins glass.
Shake the gin, lemon juice and sugar syrup with ice.
Strain into the ice-filled glass.
Top with soda water and stir briefly.
Garnish with an orange wheel and cherry.
cocktails.history:
The Collins is usually traced to John Collins, head waiter at Limmer's Hotel on Conduit Street in London, whose coffee house was known for its Gin Punch in the early 1800s. Difford's Guide suggests the Collins evolved from that punch. Harry Johnson's 1882 manual listed a John Collins with Dutch genever and a Tom Collins made with Old Tom gin, a lightly sweetened style of gin.

Other explanations abound, including a bartender at a New York tavern and American claims from San Francisco to New Jersey. In 1874 the 'Great Tom Collins Hoax' swept New York, a prank in which people were told a man called Tom Collins had insulted them and could be found in a nearby bar. Over time the base spirit shifted from genever to Old Tom to London dry gin.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Tall, crisp and lemony. Old Tom gin brings soft juniper and botanicals with a slightly rounder, sweeter texture than London dry. Fresh lemon juice gives a clean sour tang, balanced by sugar syrup into something like a sparkling, grown-up lemonade. A generous top of soda and plenty of ice keep it light and effervescent, and the orange and cherry garnish adds a touch of fruity aroma.

cocktails.name: Vesper
instructions: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
The Vesper comes from fiction rather than a bar. Ian Fleming wrote it into his first James Bond novel, Casino Royale, published in 1953. In the book Bond orders three measures of Gordon's gin, one of vodka and half a measure of Kina Lillet, shaken until ice-cold with a large slice of lemon peel, and announces he will name it once he finds a worthy title. He later names it after Vesper Lynd, who turns out to be a double agent.

Fleming drafted the novel at his Goldeneye home in Jamaica in early 1952, where he reportedly served guests a rum drink called 'Vespers'. Difford's Guide also notes the theory that Vesper Lynd was inspired by SOE agent Christine Granville. Because the original Kina Lillet is no longer made, modern versions such as the IBA's use Lillet Blanc.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Crisp, dry and powerful. Gin's juniper and botanicals lead, while the smaller measure of vodka softens and smooths the spirit without adding flavour of its own. Lillet Blanc contributes a gentle honeyed, citrusy and lightly bitter wine note that rounds the edges. Shaken very cold, the drink is clean and bracing, almost crystalline, and the lemon zest adds a bright, oily citrus aroma.

cocktails.name: Vieux Carré
instructions: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
The Vieux Carré was created in 1938 by Walter Bergeron, head bartender at the Hotel Monteleone in New Orleans, in the lounge now known as the Carousel Bar. He named it after the city's French Quarter, whose old French name translates as 'old square'. The recipe was published the same year in Stanley Clisby Arthur's book Famous New Orleans Drinks and How to Mix 'Em.

Arthur's version combined equal measures of rye whiskey, cognac and Italian vermouth with a little Bénédictine and a dash each of Peychaud's and Angostura bitters, finished with a lemon twist. The drink draws on the city's love of rye and cognac seen in the Sazerac, mixed with the vermouth of a Manhattan, making it a true New Orleans signature.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Rich, spicy and complex. Rye whiskey adds peppery grain, cognac brings soft fruit and roundness, and sweet vermouth contributes dark, wine-like sweetness. A small amount of Bénédictine layers in honey and herbal notes, while Peychaud's bitters add anise and cherry. Stirred and cold, it feels like a deeper, more herbal Manhattan, with a long, warming finish touched by orange from the garnish.

cocktails.name: Whiskey Sour
cocktails.glass: Cobbler Glass (or Old Fashioned On The Rocks)
cocktails.garnish: Half orange slice and maraschino cherry (or orange zest)
instructions: Add all ingredients to a shaker filled with ice.
Shake well (a little harder if using egg white).
Strain into a cobbler glass, or into an ice-filled old fashioned glass to serve on the rocks.
cocktails.history:
Sours, combining spirit, citrus and sugar, are among the oldest families of mixed drinks, and the Brandy Sour may once have been the more popular member. The earliest known mention of a Whiskey Sour dates from 1870, though no individual creator is known. By 1883 a Chicago bartender was describing customers who expected a float of claret on their sours, a variation now known as the New York Sour.

The Whiskey Sour came into its own during Prohibition, when it became the best-loved sour of all. Adding egg white is also an old habit: Robert Vermeire's 1922 book recommended a few drops to improve any sour. The drink now even has its own day, celebrated on 25 August.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Balanced, tangy and approachable. Bourbon brings caramel, vanilla and oak, while fresh lemon juice adds a bright, mouth-watering sourness and sugar syrup smooths the edges. With a little egg white the texture turns soft and silky with a light foam on top. The result is sweet-tart and warming at once, with the whiskey's richness still clear and a gentle citrus finish.

cocktails.name: White Lady
instructions: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake well.
Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
cocktails.history:
The first drink called a White Lady is credited to Harry MacElhone at Ciro's Club in London in 1919, but it was quite different: brandy, crème de menthe and Cointreau. His family later said he reinvented it with gin at Harry's New York Bar in Paris in 1929, though Difford's Guide finds no evidence for this. The Savoy instead credits Harry Craddock of its American Bar, whose 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book printed a gin version.

Difford's Guide favours Victor Cabrin of London's Grosvenor House as the most likely creator of the gin White Lady, citing a 1946 newspaper article that says he invented it in 1929. Early recipes had no egg white; it first appeared in a White Lady recipe in 1936 and in a specialist bar book a decade later.
cocktails.tasteProfile: Clean, crisp and citrusy. Gin gives a dry juniper and botanical backbone, while triple sec adds sweet orange and a smooth, slightly fuller body. Fresh lemon juice brings a sharp, refreshing sourness that keeps the drink bright. Served ice-cold and straight up, it tastes elegant and zesty, a gin-based cousin of the Sidecar, with a dry, lingering orange-lemon finish.
